messages.subject: gl2geno - unclear format output
parts:
Hi,
I have been trying to use the function "gl2geno"to convert a genlight filtered SNPs dataset (187 individuals, 15092 SNPs) into a .geno format, which I need to use the snmf function in LEA (admixture analysis).

However, I am quite confused on the .geno format & on how the gl2geno function converts the genotype information of a genlight object into a .geno format file.

As far as I understood from the description of the .geno format given in the LEA package (https://rdrr.io/bioc/LEA/man/geno.html), the .geno format has SNPs in rows & individuals' genotypes in columns.

However, when I tried looking at the outcome of the gl2geno function on the testset.gl genlight object provided within dartR, I find some incongruence with this definition:
  • the testset.gl is a genlight object with 250 individuals & 255 SNPs
  • when transformed into .geno format with the gl2geno function, i get a "testset.gl_geno_file" with 250 rows (corresponding to individuals) & 222 columns (which should correspond to the SNPs...although the original genlight object had 255 SNPs..)
So, in the .geno "testset.gl_geno_file" obtained through gl2geno:
  1. not only the SNPs are in columns and not in rows - as described by LEA package for the .geno format
  2. the number of SNPs of the original genlight object (255 SNPs) do not correspond to the ncol of the .geno file obtained with gl2geno (222 col)
Am I missing something?
I am still confused as to how the .geno format is supposed to be structures, as in this link https://uqrmaie1.github.io/admixtools/articles/io.html the Eigenstrat .geno format is described as having 1 row per SNP & 1 col per each individual....which is the correct form of the .geno file??

When I try to convert my own genlight object (187 individuals, 15092 SNPs) to a .geno file with gl2geno, I obtain a "matrix array" object with 187 rows & 15092 columns - corresponding to a format with individuals in rows & SNPs in columns, and the number of individuals & SNPs correspond to the nInd & nLoc of the original genlight object.

Once I understand how the .geno format is structured and obtained, I would like to ind a way to combine the population information of each individual to the .geno file in order to plot the Q ancestry coefficients (obtained through the LEA::snmf function) by populations and not only by K clusters...but in order to do that I need to understand how the .geno file is structured and obtained and whether I can just combine the population metadata from the genlight object to the Q matrix obtain from LEA:snmf on the .geno file...

I would appreciate any clarification and input on this matter!

Hi Gabriella,

1. As described in the link you shared (https://rdrr.io/bioc/LEA/man/geno.html), in the geno format, SNPs are in rows, and individuals are in columns. An example of a geno file with three individuals and four loci should look like this:

112
010
091
121

You can verify this by opening your geno file in a text editor. The read.geno function transposes the information of the file, so SNPs are in columns and individuals are in rows.

2. When a reference genome is not available, the choice of the reference allele is arbitrary. DArT assigns the reference allele to the allele with the higher frequency in the dataset, which is the usual approach. As long as the same reference allele is used for genotyping all the individuals, the choice of the reference allele has no implications in the analysis of SNPs.

3. There was a bug in the function that filtered out some loci, which I fixed. To use this updated version of the function you should install the developing version of dartR by typing in the R console:
> library(dartR)
> gl.install.vanilla.dartR(flavour = "dev")

Cheers,
Luis

2.1 Most methods based on population genetics assume that loci are independent of each other, even if they don't acknowledge it directly. In other words, models assume that loci are inherited by offspring as independent units from their parents (due to random mating, independent assortment of chromosomes and recombination). 1. As described in the link you shared (https://rdrr.io/bioc/LEA/man/geno.html), in the geno format, SNPs are in rows, and individuals are in columns. An example of a geno file with three individuals and four loci should look like this:

112
010
091
121

2. When a reference genome is not available, the choice of the reference allele is arbitrary. DArT assigns the reference allele to the allele with the higher frequency in the dataset, which is the usual approach. As long as the same reference allele is used for genotyping all the individuals, the choice of the reference allele has no implications in the analysis of SNPs.

      2.1 Most methods based on population genetics assume that loci are independent of each other, even if they don't acknowledge it directly. In other words, models assume that loci are inherited by offspring as independent units from their parents (due to random mating, independent assortment of chromosomes and recombination). This is not always true. For example, search for "linked selection". That's why it does not matter what allele is the reference and which is the alternative. Also, that's why it is important to filter loci in linkage disequilibrium. By the way, early next week, we will have ready a nice function to filter loci in LD. It is also important to read and understand the theory behind the method you are using and the question you are trying to answer.       - Dementieva N, Mitrofanova O, Dysin A, Kudinov A, Stanishevskaya O, Larkina T, et al. Assessing the effects of rare alleles and linkage disequilibrium on estimates of genetic diversity in the chicken populations. Animal. 2021;15(3):100171.
      - Schmidt TL, Jasper ME, Weeks AR, Hoffmann AA. Unbiased population heterozygosity estimates from genome‐wide sequence data. Methods in Ecology and Evolution. 2021;12(10):1888-98.

      2.1 Most methods based on population genetics assume that loci are independent of each other, even if they don't acknowledge it directly. This is not always true. For example, search for "linked selection". That's why it does not matter what allele is the reference and which is the alternative. Also, that's why it is important to filter loci in linkage disequilibrium. By the way, early next week, we will have ready a nice function to filter loci in LD.       112
      010
      091
      121

      2. When a reference genome is not available, the choice of the reference allele is arbitrary. DArT assigns the reference allele to the allele with the higher frequency in the dataset, which is the usual approach. As long as the same reference allele is used for genotyping all the individuals, the choice of the reference allele has no implications in the analysis of SNPs.

      2.1 Most methods based on population genetics assume that loci are independent of each other, even if they don't acknowledge it directly. In other words, models assume that loci are inherited by offspring as independent units from their parents (due to random mating, independent assortment of chromosomes and recombination). This is not always true. For example, search for "linked selection". That's why it does not matter what allele is the reference and which is the alternative. Also, that's why it is important to filter loci in linkage disequilibrium. By the way, early next week, we will have ready a nice function to filter loci in LD.       - Dementieva N, Mitrofanova O, Dysin A, Kudinov A, Stanishevskaya O, Larkina T, et al. Assessing the effects of rare alleles and linkage disequilibrium on estimates of genetic diversity in the chicken populations. Animal. 2021;15(3):100171.
      - Schmidt TL, Jasper ME, Weeks AR, Hoffmann AA. Unbiased population heterozygosity estimates from genome‐wide sequence data. Methods in Ecology and Evolution. 2021;12(10):1888-98.

      010
      091
      121

      2. When a reference genome is not available, the choice of the reference allele is arbitrary. DArT assigns the reference allele to the allele with the higher frequency in the dataset, which is the usual approach. As long as the same reference allele is used for genotyping all the individuals, the choice of the reference allele has no implications in the analysis of SNPs.

Hi Gabriella,

1. As described in the link you shared (https://rdrr.io/bioc/LEA/man/geno.html), in the geno format, SNPs are in rows, and individuals are in columns. An example of a geno file with three individuals and four loci should look like this:

112
010
091
121

You can verify this by opening your geno file in a text editor. The read.geno function transposes the information of the file, so SNPs are in columns and individuals are in rows.

2. When a reference genome is not available, the choice of the reference allele is arbitrary. DArT assigns the reference allele to the allele with the higher frequency in the dataset, which is the usual approach. As long as the same reference allele is used for genotyping all the individuals, the choice of the reference allele has no implications in the analysis of SNPs.

3. There was a bug in the function that filtered out some loci, which I fixed. To use this updated version of the function you should install the developing version of dartR by typing in the R console:
> library(dartR)
> gl.install.vanilla.dartR(flavour = "dev")

Cheers,
Luis
